lines.orig: GPT-family models, like those behind ChatGPT, run TinyGPT's loop: read the tokens, score every possible next one, pick, append, repeat. And they're built from the same kinds of blocks.
lines.visuals: TinyGPT's loop as boxes: tokens → embed → [attention → MLP] × 3 layers → probabilities → pick one, with an arrow looping back ('append it & repeat'). GPT-family models (GPT-2, GPT-3, the models behind ChatGPT) use the same loop and block types, often with variations (RoPE, GQA, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, MoE).
lines.new: How far is our tiny model from ChatGPT? Here is TinyGPT's loop. It reads the tokens, small chunks of text, and scores every possible next one. Then it picks one, appends it, and repeats. GPT-family models, like those behind ChatGPT, run this same loop. And they're built from the same kinds of blocks.

lines.orig: The big difference is scale. GPT-2 ranged from 124 million to 1.5 billion parameters. GPT-3 had 175 billion, 96 layers, and a 2,048-token context instead of 64.
lines.visuals: Log-scale bar chart of published parameter counts: TinyGPT 170,560 (3 layers, width 64), GPT-2 small 124M (12 layers, width 768), GPT-2 XL 1.5B (48 layers, width 1,600), GPT-3 175B (96 layers, width 12,288, context 2,048). GPT-3 ≈ 1,026,032 × TinyGPT.
lines.new: The big difference is scale. Each bar counts a model's parameters, the numbers it learns. GPT-2 ranged from 124 million to 1.5 billion parameters. GPT-3 had 175 billion, with 96 layers. Its context, the text it can see at once, was 2,048 tokens instead of TinyGPT's 64.

lines.orig: Stage one, pretraining: TinyGPT's game, on a huge pile of web text. GPT-3 trained on about 300 billion tokens; TinyGPT on 12 million. The result is a base model: an autocomplete that may just continue your question.
lines.visuals: Log-scale bars of tokens processed in training: TinyGPT 12,288,000 (7.3 passes over its 1,686,858-token corpus) vs GPT-3 ≈ 300 billion (published). Compute ≈ 6·N·D: 1.26e+13 vs 3.14e23 FLOPs. Illustration: a base model continuing 'Q: What is the capital of France?' with more questions instead of answering.
lines.new: Making a chatbot takes three stages. Stage one is pretraining: TinyGPT's game of guessing the next token, played on a huge pile of web text. GPT-3 trained on about 300 billion tokens, and TinyGPT on 12 million. The result is a base model: an autocomplete that may just continue your question. Here it adds more questions instead of answering.

lines.orig: Stage two: supervised fine-tuning. Same loss, now on example conversations written by people: a request, and a good response. The model learns to play the assistant.
lines.visuals: Illustrative training example: PERSON 'Explain photosynthesis to a ten-year-old.' / ASSISTANT 'Plants catch sunlight…'. The reply is underlined: the loss is usually computed on the reply tokens only.
lines.new: Stage two is supervised fine-tuning, an extra round of training. It uses the same loss, the score for how wrong the guesses are. But now it trains on example conversations written by people: a request, and a good response. The model learns to play the assistant.

lines.orig: Stage three, preference tuning. People rank several answers; a reward model learns their taste, then scores the chat model's own answers, and reinforcement learning nudges it toward high reward, without drifting too far. That's RLHF.
lines.visuals: RLHF diagram (illustrative answers): labelers rank several answers per prompt (4–9 in InstructGPT) → a reward model learns the rankings → the chat model writes answers, the reward model scores them, reinforcement learning (PPO) nudges it toward high reward, plus a KL penalty for drifting from the SFT model. Citation: InstructGPT, Ouyang et al. 2022.
lines.new: Stage three is preference tuning. People rank several answers to one prompt. From those rankings, a reward model learns their taste. It then scores the chat model's own answers, and reinforcement learning uses those scores. Learning by trial and reward, it nudges the chat model toward high reward, without drifting too far from its stage two version. That's RLHF: reinforcement learning from human feedback.

lines.orig: In the InstructGPT paper, labelers preferred answers from a 1.3 billion parameter model tuned this way over the 175 billion GPT-3.
lines.visuals: InstructGPT result (Ouyang et al. 2022): outputs of the 1.3B InstructGPT were preferred by labelers over the 175B GPT-3, despite over 100× fewer parameters. Footnote: newer methods such as DPO (2023) skip the separate reward model.
lines.new: How much does this help? In the InstructGPT paper, human labelers compared answers. They preferred a 1.3 billion parameter model tuned this way over the 175 billion GPT-3, which is more than a hundred times bigger.

lines.orig: And a chat is still one long document. Special tokens mark who's speaking, and the model keeps predicting next tokens until it predicts the end-of-turn token itself.
lines.visuals: A conversation laid out as one token stream in a ChatML-style template: <|im_start|>system … <|im_end|> <|im_start|>user What color is the sky?<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant, then the model's reply (teal) generated until it emits <|im_end|>.
lines.new: And under the hood, a chat is still one long document. Special tokens, markers that aren't ordinary text, show who's speaking. And the model keeps predicting next tokens, which form its reply, until it predicts the end-of-turn token itself. That's how it knows when to stop.

lines.orig: Generation's speed trick is the KV cache. Old keys and values never change, so keep them, and process only the newest position. For 8 new tokens: 30 positions instead of 212, same result.
lines.visuals: Two grids, one row per generation step (8 new tokens after the 23-token probe prompt). Without cache every step recomputes all positions (212 total); with the KV cache earlier keys/values are reused (blue outlines) and only the new token is computed (30 total). Real check on TinyGPT: logits match to 5.2e-06.
lines.new: Generating text has a speed trick: the KV cache. In attention, later tokens look back at each earlier token's key and value, the K and V. Those old keys and values never change, so keep them, and process only the newest position. For 8 new tokens, that's 30 positions instead of 212, with the same result.

lines.orig: Then the sampling knobs. Temperature divides the logits: below one sharpens, red to 96 percent; above one flattens, red to 72. Top-p keeps the fewest tokens covering 90 percent: here, red and white.
lines.visuals: Real TinyGPT probabilities after the probe prompt as temperature changes: at T = 0.7 ' red' 96.2%, at T = 1.0 87.1%, at T = 1.3 72.2%. Top-p 0.9 keeps ' red' + ' white' = 93.0%.
lines.new: Then there are the sampling knobs, which control how the next token is picked. Temperature divides the logits, the raw scores, before they become probabilities. A temperature below one sharpens the choice: red gets 96 percent. Above one flattens it: red gets only 72 percent. Top-p keeps the fewest tokens that together cover 90 percent: here, red and white.

lines.orig: So: the same core loop. GPT-3 was a million times bigger, plus refinements and far more text, then tuned into an assistant. The core ideas, you've seen inside TinyGPT.
lines.visuals: Recap: the same pipeline (tokens → embed → [attention → MLP] × 96 layers for GPT-3 → probabilities → pick one) plus: GPT-3 had ~a million times the weights, web-scale pretraining, instruction & preference tuning, refinements (RoPE, GQA, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, MoE), chat tokens, KV cache and sampling knobs. CTA: open the X-ray.
lines.new: So, to sum up: models like ChatGPT run the same core loop as TinyGPT. GPT-3 was about a million times bigger, with some refinements and far more text. Then it was tuned into an assistant. The core ideas, you've already seen inside TinyGPT.
